---
title: "Performance and caching"
---

Two fixed costs stand between a fresh session and a prediction, the download of the weights from
Hugging Face and the JAX compilation of the network, and both are paid once per session. The
compilation is paid again for each new batch size. Prediction itself is orders of magnitude
cheaper than either of those, and cheaper still per scenario when the scenarios are handed over
in a single batch rather than one call at a time.

## Setup cost

`preload_models` warms everything the pipeline needs, loading the three estiMINT
gradient-boosted models and both stateMINT checkpoints. It downloads them if they are not
already cached.

```{python}
import time
from estimint import preload_models

t0 = time.perf_counter()
eir_models, emulator_models = preload_models()
print(f"preload_models: {time.perf_counter() - t0:.2f} s")
print("estiMINT :", list(eir_models))
print("stateMINT:", list(emulator_models))
```

Call it once at the top of a script or a notebook. On a cold machine most of that time is the
download, roughly 38 MB per predictor. On a warm one it is deserialisation from disk. Note that
`preload_models` tracks `main` rather than a pinned tag, so load the checkpoints yourself with
[`from_pretrained(..., revision=...)`](the-emulator.qmd) when the exact weights matter.

## The cache

Weights land in the standard Hugging Face cache. Every later load reads from it.

```{python}
from huggingface_hub import constants

print(constants.HF_HUB_CACHE)
```

Two environment variables control the cache. Both must be set before the first import.

| Variable | Effect |
|---|---|
| `HF_HOME` | Relocates the whole cache. Point it at a shared or scratch filesystem on a cluster, where a home directory quota will not hold 80 MB of weights. |
| `HF_HUB_OFFLINE=1` | Forbids network access. Loads succeed from the cache and fail loudly otherwise. Set it on a compute node with no outbound route, and pre-populate the cache from the login node. |

```bash
export HF_HOME=/scratch/$USER/hf
export HF_HUB_OFFLINE=1
```

## Batching

`.predict` is a single compiled forward pass over the whole batch, and because JAX compiles the
network on first use and recompiles it whenever the batch size changes, a loop of fifty
single-scenario calls performs fifty separate forward passes and gets none of the parallelism
the hardware can give.

```{python}
import numpy as np
from stateMINT.model import Mamba2Regressor

prevalence = Mamba2Regressor.from_pretrained(
    "dide-ic/stateMINT", predictor="prevalence", revision="v1.2.2",
)

district = {
    "eir": 31.96, "dn0_use": 0.311, "dn0_future": 0.485,
    "Q0": 0.85, "phi_bednets": 0.80, "seasonal": 0,
    "routine": 0.0, "itn_use": 0.70, "irs_use": 0.0,
    "itn_future": 0.70, "irs_future": 0.0, "lsm": 0.0,
}

batch = [dict(district, eir=float(e)) for e in np.linspace(5, 60, 50)]
len(batch)
```

The first call pays the compilation cost. The second does not.

```{python}
t0 = time.perf_counter()
prevalence.predict(batch)
first = time.perf_counter() - t0

t0 = time.perf_counter()
prevalence.predict(batch)
second = time.perf_counter() - t0

print(f"first call  (compile + run): {first * 1000:7.0f} ms")
print(f"second call (run only)     : {second * 1000:7.0f} ms")
```

The same fifty scenarios then run as fifty separate calls, each compiled for a batch of one.

```{python}
prevalence.predict([district])          # pay the batch-of-one compilation

t0 = time.perf_counter()
for scenario in batch:
    prevalence.predict([scenario])
looped = time.perf_counter() - t0

print(f"one call, 50 scenarios : {second * 1000:7.0f} ms   ({second / 50 * 1000:.1f} ms each)")
print(f"50 calls, 1 scenario   : {looped * 1000:7.0f} ms   ({looped / 50 * 1000:.1f} ms each)")
print(f"speed-up               : {looped / second:.1f}x")
```

Notice that the second call costs a small fraction of the first, and that the fifty looped calls
cost several times the one batched call doing the same work. This is because a call enters the
compiled forward pass once, whatever the batch size. The loop pays it fifty times over.

Build the whole list first, then call `.predict` once. A grid of a few hundred rows is still a
single call, and still under a second. Note that the timings printed above came off whatever
machine rendered the cells. The durable part of the comparison is the ratio between one batched
call and fifty looped ones, not the absolute milliseconds.

## CPU and GPU

The timings above are CPU timings, and a CPU is entirely adequate at the scale of a scenario grid,
since the emulator is small, two Mamba2 layers with `d_model` 256. There is no reason to reach for
a GPU to compare a dozen campaigns. On a GPU the same forward pass is roughly six times faster,
measured on an NVIDIA L40S, and both sit several orders of magnitude below the minutes a
`malariasimulation` run of the same twelve simulated years takes. The measurements, and what the
speed costs in accuracy, are in [Accuracy and speed](../03-concepts/validation.qmd).

For a sweep of thousands of scenarios, a CUDA 12 build of JAX is available as an extra.

```bash
pip install "mintstate[gpu]"
```

Nothing in the API changes when a GPU is present. JAX places the computation on the accelerator
if it finds one, and without a CUDA-enabled JAX installed it falls back to CPU and warns. Note
that the warning is the only sign that the GPU is not in use, so read it rather than suppress it.
